I've been learning category theory on and off for about three years. I'm a self-learner, and it's been a while since I finished my undergraduate degree in mathematics.

I'm working on my proof-writing and trying to get a solid grasp of categorical products. I'd appreciate any feedback from the community. As a self learner, it's hard to tell whether i'm right track.

My proof aims to show that the Category of Sets has a Product AxB with the universal property.
However, I could only accomplish this by peeking into elements of the sets, which feels a little naughty in CT.
Outside of feedback on my proof, I'm curious if there is a way to prove this without using elements?

I welcome any and all feedback, whether it's about correctness, rigor, or style.
Thank you in advanced!

Proof

Claim. Set\mathbf{Set}Set has a product A×BA \times BA×B satisfying the universal property.

Given:
- A×B∈Ob(Set)A \times B \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{Set})A×B∈Ob(Set), with π1:A×B→A\pi_1 : A \times B \to Aπ1​:A×B→A and π2:A×B→B\pi_2 : A \times B \to Bπ2​:A×B→B
- P′∈Ob(Set)P' \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{Set})P′∈Ob(Set), with f:P′→Af : P' \to Af:P′→A and g:P′→Bg : P' \to Bg:P′→B

Goal: there exists a unique m:P′→A×Bm : P' \to A \times Bm:P′→A×B such that

f=π1∘m,g=π2∘mf = \pi_1 \circ m, \qquad g = \pi_2 \circ mf=π1​∘m,g=π2​∘m

Existence. For z∈P′z \in P'z∈P′, define m:P′→A×Bm : P' \to A \times Bm:P′→A×B by m(z)=(f(z),g(z))m(z) = (f(z), g(z))m(z)=(f(z),g(z)). Then

(π1∘m)(z)=π1(m(z))=f(z)(π2∘m)(z)=π2(m(z))=g(z)\begin{aligned} (\pi_1 \circ m)(z) &= \pi_1(m(z)) = f(z) \\ (\pi_2 \circ m)(z) &= \pi_2(m(z)) = g(z) \end{aligned}(π1​∘m)(z)(π2​∘m)(z)​=π1​(m(z))=f(z)=π2​(m(z))=g(z)​

Hence such an m exists!

Uniqueness. Suppose there are such morphisms m,m′:P′→A×Bm, m' : P' \to A \times Bm,m′:P′→A×B both satisfying

f=π1∘m,g=π2∘m,f=π1∘m′,g=π2∘m′f = \pi_1 \circ m,\quad g = \pi_2 \circ m,\quad f = \pi_1 \circ m',\quad g = \pi_2 \circ m'f=π1​∘m,g=π2​∘m,f=π1​∘m′,g=π2​∘m′

Then

m′(z)=(π1(m′(z)),π2(m′(z)))=(f(z),g(z))=(π1((m(z)),π2((m(z)))=m(z)m'(z) = (\pi_1(m'(z)),\pi_2(m'(z))) = (f(z),g(z)) = (\pi_1((m(z)),\pi_2((m(z))) = m(z)m′(z)=(π1​(m′(z)),π2​(m′(z)))=(f(z),g(z))=(π1​((m(z)),π2​((m(z)))=m(z)

Therefore mmm is unique.

There is no problem with examining the elements of sets when proving the existence of constructs like products in the particular category Set, as long as you've defined Set in such a way that sets actually have elements, anyway. This is just setting up the concrete basis of the abstractions you're going to use later.

I think one would, then, usually define what the elements of A×BA \times BA×B are, at least by reference before constructing the product projections π1\pi_1π1​ and π2\pi_2π2​ (which you also don't seem to do here, just kind of assume) and the pairing on functions.

There's also a problem with the proof of uniqueness: you assume both mmm and m′m'm′ are of the form given in the Existence proof. It's okay to assume it for one of them since then you're proving that the other is equal to the one you constructed, which establishes uniqueness, but proving that two of the exact thing you constructed are equal doesn't establish much.

The essential facts you need to take advantage of to establish uniqueness are that if π1((x,y))=x′\pi_1((x,y)) = x'π1​((x,y))=x′ then x=x′x = x'x=x′ and if π2((x,y))=y′\pi_2((x,y)) = y'π2​((x,y))=y′, then y=y′y = y'y=y′. That will allow you to prove that m′(z)=m(z)m'(z) = m(z)m′(z)=m(z) without making any assumption on what m′(z)m'(z)m′(z) is other than that it is an element of A×BA \times BA×B.

Welcome to this zulip, @Christopher Boon ! I hope you find the community here helpful and interesting!

Regarding the use of elements: In my experience, if I'm trying to prove that a category has products (or some other feature!), it's a good thing to incorporate things I know about that category in my argument. Since the objects of Set\mathsf{Set}Set have elements, in my opinion it's sensible to use elements when reasoning in that setting.

That being said, I can remember also feeling that elements aren't quite in the categorical spirit. I found it interesting to learn that one can often understand "elements" as certain morphisms. For example, in the category of sets, the elements of a set AAA correspond to functions :1→A:1 \to A:1→A, where 111 is some set with a single element. I felt this was more in the "relational" spirit, where we study objects in terms of the morphisms relating them.

I'll also add that in addition to functions 1→A1 \to A1→A, which we consider "elements of AAA" (sometimes called "global elements), we have functions X→AX \to AX→A for some arbitrary object XXX. We call these "generalized elements" (of shape XXX, if we want to be clear about the domain), and you can reason about them almost exactly how you would reason about ordinary elements.

The benefit, though, is that if you reason with generalized elements, then your arguments will still hold even in categories where the actual notion of "element" doesn't exist, or doesn't capture the full structure of the object. This is basically a consequence of the Yoneda lemma.

With practice lots and lots of "elementwise" proofs that work in the category of sets can be adapted to work in arbitrary categories by working with generalized elements, or possibly passing first to categories of presheaves and then reflecting back using Yoneda. Hopefully this is encouragement that working elementwise is a totally ok thing to do, especially when starting out!

Thank you all for your insights, this is very enlightening and encouraging. I updated my proof, and I will continue to chew on your comments as I delve in/practice more. Your feedback means a lot to me!

Two questions that came to mind:
1) What if we are working in a Category where the exact details of the Product are not clear. Can we show it exists another way? Something like showing some there's some limit-preserving map... and if products exist in the first then they exist in the destination category. Unsure here, as (co)limits and adjunct functors are next in my learning roadmap.

2) As far as functions 1→A1 \rightarrow A1→A and X→AX \rightarrow AX→A are concerned, this is truly an interesting perspective! I had encountered the universal construction of Terminal objects in Set, which implies A→1A \rightarrow 1A→1 from all (non-troublesome) objects AAA. I convinced myself that morphisms to the terminal object in Set is a way of "selecting elements". But 1→A1 \rightarrow A1→A looks to have it's arrow reversed, and has the flavor of SetopSet^{op}Setop. This duality is not quite clear in my head. Any suggestions on what to explore here?

Re 1) Yes, and there are many ways to do this. Here is an important example. In your "roadmap" you will surely soon see that for any two categories C\mathbf{C}C and D\mathbf{D}D, if D\mathbf{D}D has products (in fact any type of (co)limit), then so does the category of functors from C\mathbf{C}C to D\mathbf{D}D. Thus, if you can show your category is some kind of category of functors whose codomains has products, then your category has products too.

Re 2) 111 being terminal in Set\mathbf{Set}Set means that there is one and exactly one function !A:A→1{!_A}: \mathbf{A} \rightarrow 1!A​:A→1 for all objects AAA. There is no troublesome AAA, and the function !A!_A!A​ is unique. This is because 111 is a singleton set, it contains a single element so the function !A!_A!A​ has to send every a∈Aa \in Aa∈A to that element. (You may think ∅\emptyset∅ is troublesome because there is no element to send, but !∅!_{\emptyset}!∅​ is still defined in the same way, just that there is no a∈∅a \in \emptyseta∈∅ to act on.)

Reversing the arrow, a function 1→A1 \rightarrow A1→A must send the unique element of the singleton to some a∈Aa \in Aa∈A. There are as many choices as there are elements of AAA. So we think of such functions as "selecting an element in AAA": it selects the element that is the image of the unique element in 111.

There is a duality here only in that we are reversing the arrows. There is no abstract duality between "selecting elements" and being terminal because the situation in Set\mathbf{Set}Set does not generalize to other categories. First, because in many categories, the notion of element is unclear (e.g. the category corresponding to the poset (N,≤)(\N,\leq)(N,≤)). Second, because even in some concrete categories whose objects have clearly defined elements, e.g. Mon\mathbf{Mon}Mon or $\mathbf{Grp}or or or\mathbf{Ring}$$, elements do not correspond to morphisms 1→A1 \rightarrow A1→A, where 111 is the terminal object of these categories. In these three categories, there is a unique morphism 1→A1 \rightarrow A1→A for any monoid/group/ring AAA. This means 111 is also initial, we often call it a zero object because it is both terminal and initial.
